story.title: When Fingers Become Eyes: How Ceramicist Mousa Al Balushi Shapes Clay Through Inner Sight
story.seo_title: Mousa Al Balushi: Omani Blind Ceramic Sculptor | OmanSpire
story.meta_description: Discover how blind Omani ceramicist Mousa bin Badr Al Balushi shapes clay through touch and sensory memory into contemporary sculptures rooted in Omani heritage.

detail.extracted_title: When Fingers Become Eyes: How Ceramicist Mousa Al Balushi Shapes Clay Through Inner Sight
detail.excerpt: Blind since early childhood, the Omani sculptor turns memory, touch, and patience into stoneware vessels and expressive figures that speak across galleries in Muscat and the Gulf.
detail.article_html:
Before Mousa bin Badr Al Balushi begins a new sculpture, his hands rest quietly on the damp block of clay. He checks its cool temperature, presses lightly to judge the moisture held inside the earth, and tests how far the material will bend before cracking. Blind since early childhood, Al Balushi has spent years learning the language of clay through touch, patience, and sensory memory—turning a material dug from the ground into expressive ceramic works exhibited across Oman and the Gulf.

From Omar bin Al Khattab Institute to the Ceramic Studio

Al Balushi's relationship with ceramics began during his youth. He studied at the Omar bin Al Khattab Institute for the Blind, where he completed his secondary schooling before going on to earn a university degree and take up a post in a government department. Alongside his daily work, clay offered him an open space where thoughts and unspoken emotions could take physical form.

Working with ceramics without sight requires a disciplined sequence of movements. Both hands must move in steady coordination: one palm supports the inner wall of the vessel while the fingers of the other shape the outer curve. Every stage—from wedging and molding to drying and kiln firing—demands close attention to how the clay responds. When a piece shifts or cracks in the heat, Al Balushi treats the setback as part of the craft's natural conversation, adjusting his pressure and timing on the next form.

Vessels of Heritage and Figures of Quiet Reflection

Omani heritage runs deep through Al Balushi's studio practice. Rather than copying traditional water jars and incense burners as museum replicas, he draws on their familiar curves and surface carvings to build contemporary sculptures.

In Whisper of Clay (Hams Al-Teen), traditional Omani motifs emerge through warm, hand-carved relief. Another work, Vase of Life (Mazhariyat Al-Hayat), rises in calm white tones from a simple base, opening upward like a desert bloom. In his animal and figurative pieces, the forms grow bolder: The Flamingo captures the poised curve of a bird's neck and layered feathers, while Defying the Impossible (Tahaddi Al-Mustaheel) balances a rearing horse on its hind legs to express motion and freedom.

Perhaps his most intimate work is Embracing Silence (Ihtidan Al-Samt), a sculpture of a seated man resting his cheek against his palm. Rippling, wave-like lines wrap around the lower body, suggesting the quiet current of memory and inward thought that needs no spoken words.

Sharing the Craft Beyond Muscat

Over the past several years, Al Balushi has presented his ceramics at local and regional exhibitions, including the My Disability Will Not Stop Me showcase in Kuwait and the Muscat Art exhibition held at the end of October. Visitors often pause beside his table, surprised that works of such proportion and surface detail were shaped entirely by touch.

For Al Balushi, each exhibition is an opportunity to speak directly to young Omanis and people with disabilities who may be holding back their own creative talents. His advice is grounded in the slow, steady rhythm of the potter's table: start with what is in your hands, give every stage the time it needs, and never measure your own path against someone else's stride.

detail.instagram_caption:
Before Mousa bin Badr Al Balushi begins a new sculpture, his hands rest quietly on the damp block of clay to judge its moisture, temperature, and pliability. Blind since early childhood, the Omani ceramicist has spent years mastering the language of clay through touch, sensory memory, and patience—shaping raw earth into expressive contemporary sculptures exhibited in Muscat and Kuwait.

A graduate of the Omar bin Al Khattab Institute for the Blind who went on to complete his university studies and join the civil service, Al Balushi draws on traditional Omani pottery forms and natural motifs to create works such as Whisper of Clay, Vase of Life, Defying the Impossible, and Embracing Silence. From delicate surface relief to a rearing horse balanced on its hind legs, every curve is guided by the coordinated rhythm of his hands through molding, drying, and kiln firing.

Through his participation in showcases including Muscat Art and regional exhibitions in the Gulf, Al Balushi encourages young Omanis with disabilities to trust their own pace and develop their craft step by step.

slides.h: Touch and sensory memory guide every stage from raw clay to the kiln.
p: Blind since early childhood, Omani ceramicist [[Mousa bin Badr Al Balushi]] reads the moisture, elasticity, and warmth of raw clay through his fingertips—coordinating both hands across {{molding, drying, and high-heat firing}}.

slides.h: Omani pottery traditions take on contemporary sculptural forms.
p: An alumnus of the [[Omar bin Al Khattab Institute for the Blind]], Al Balushi reimagines traditional Omani earthenware in works like [[Whisper of Clay]], [[Vase of Life]], and the rearing horse sculpture {{Defying the Impossible}}.

slides.h: Clay becomes a quiet language for memory, patience, and self-expression.
quote: Ceramics are part of our history and daily life; bringing them into contemporary works preserves this heritage and presents it to new generations in a renewed artistic spirit.
Mousa bin Badr Al Balushi, Omani Ceramic Sculptor

slides.h: Regional exhibitions carry a message of perseverance to young creators.
p: From the [[My Disability Will Not Stop Me]] showcase in Kuwait to the [[Muscat Art]] exhibition, Al Balushi's sculptures demonstrate how {{steady practice and self-belief}} open unexpected doors.
